deep.reconstruction:
The page continues Gauss's table of the periods of the decimal expansions of fractions a/p with prime denominator p. Here p runs from 331 to 367; the previous page covers 271 to 317 and the next page 373 to 401. For each prime Gauss writes the residue classes of the period. Each row is the full period (repetend) of some fraction a/p. The number of rows is (p-1)/e, where e = ord_p(10) is the length of the period, so the rows together run through all p-1 nonzero numerators. In modern terms the rows are the cosets of the subgroup <10> in (Z/pZ)^*.

Prime by prime (the row and digit counts are my reading of the layout):

(1) p = 331: three rows of 110 digits each (9+2 groups of ten), so ord_331(10) = 110 and 3*110 = 330.
- Row 3 begins 0302114803 6253776435 0453172205 ... This is the period of 10/331 = 0.0302114803..., i.e. the period of 1/331 = 0.00302114803... read from its second digit.
- Row 1 begins 1450151057 ..., which matches 48/331 = 0.1450151057... (my identification).
- Row 2 begins 2960725075 ..., which matches 98/331 = 0.2960725075... (my identification).
- The red notes 'Ende | Anfang' mark where Gauss's chosen starting point of the cycle lies.

(2) p = 337: a single row of 336 digits (9+9+9 groups, then 6 groups and a final 6-digit block). So ord_337(10) = 336 and 10 is a primitive root mod 337. The row is the period of 10/337 = 0.0296735905 0445103857 ...; its true ending is ...1810089020 7715133531 157270.

(3) p = 347: two rows of 173 digits (90 + 83), so ord_347(10) = 173 and 2*173 = 346. Row 2 is the period of 10/347 = 0.0288184438 0403458213 ..., ending ...8357348703 17|0.

(4) p = 349: three rows of 116 digits (90 + 26), so ord_349(10) = 116 and 3*116 = 348. Row 3 is the period of 10/349 = 0.0286532951 2893982808 0229226361 ..., ending ...478510.

(5) p = 353: eleven rows of 32 digits each (3 groups of ten plus 2), six in the left column and five in the right. So ord_353(10) = 32 and 11*32 = 352. The last right-hand row, 0283286118 9801699716 7138810198 30, is the period of 10/353. The small numbers 4, 7, 10 and '84|85' beside the rows are Gauss's working marks, presumably row indices or checks.

(6) p = 359: two rows of 179 digits (90 + 89), so ord_359(10) = 179 and 2*179 = 358. This agrees with theory:
- (2/359) = +1, since 359 ≡ 7 mod 8.
- (5/359) = (359/5) = (4/5) = +1.
- Hence 10 is a quadratic residue, its order divides 179, and 179 is prime.
Row 2 is the period of 10/359 = 0.0278551532 0334261838 ....

(7) p = 367: one row of 366 digits (4 lines of 90, then 732970), so ord_367(10) = 366 and 10 is a primitive root mod 367. The row is the period of 10/367 = 0.0272479564 0326975476 ....

The page computes no proofs. It is pure long-division output with structural bookkeeping: periods, period lengths and coset decomposition. It serves Gauss's table for converting common fractions into decimals, in the context of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 312-318. Marginalia: 'Math 17' is the library signature, '(13)' the folio number, '2436' an archive number.
errors: No computational errors detected in the spot checks: the leading digits of 10/331, 48/331, 98/331, 10/337, 10/347, 10/349, 10/353, 10/359 and 10/367 are correct, and the period lengths are consistent with ord_p(10).

The end of the p = 337 row should read ...7715133531 157270, since the period of 1/337 ends ...7715133531 15727 and is followed by 00296.... The transcription's '1572770' is probably a misreading (doubled 7) rather than Gauss's slip; worth rechecking on the original.
The p = 353 left row 5 contains a struck-out or overwritten digit block ('9150141...'). Gauss himself corrected it; it cannot be verified from the image.

results.what: Complete decimal periods of a/p for p = 331, 337, 347, 349, 353, 359, 367, arranged by residue classes (cosets of <10> in (Z/pZ)^*), with period lengths 110, 336, 173, 116, 32, 179, 366.
results.modern_name: Table of decimal repetends / multiplicative order of 10 mod p (cyclic numbers, coset decomposition)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801, arts. 312-318; table published in Werke II); also Burckhardt, Reuschle, Desmarest for related tables

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working sheet of Gauss's well-known table of decimal periods for prime denominators below 1000, published in his Werke. The computation is routine long division, and the material is already firmly attributed to him.

transcription_corrections: p = 337 row, final block: '1572770' should almost certainly read '157270'. The true digits are ...7715133531 15727 0, which gives 336 digits in total.

p = 349 row 1, first group: the image reads '0372492836' only if one digit is miscounted. The group structure (90 + 26 = 116 digits) should be preserved when correcting; the second line is '5902578796 5616045845 272206'.
Marginal '44413' near the folio number '(13)' is uncertain; it may be '4413' or an archival mark, not part of the table.
p = 359 row 1, end of second line: the last group is probably 9 digits ('072423398'), since 90 + 89 = 179, rather than '0724233983'.
The left-margin '36' before '6713091922' is a misplaced fragment, probably the row marker or a check digit, and not part of the digit string.
